The history of lighthouses begins in antiquity, with the most famous example being the Pharos of Alexandria, built in the 3rd century BCE. This massive structure, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, utilized a fire at its peak to guide ships into the harbor, establishing the fundamental concept of a fixed light source for maritime navigation.

During the Middle Ages and early modern period, lighthouse construction remained sporadic and often relied on simple bonfires or small stone towers. It was not until the 17th and 18th centuries that systematic efforts began, particularly in Britain and France, to build more robust structures. Innovations in lens technology, such as the Fresnel lens invented in the early 19th century, dramatically increased the range and efficiency of lighthouse beams, transforming them from local markers into powerful navigational aids.

The 19th and early 20th centuries marked the golden age of lighthouse building, with thousands of structures erected worldwide to protect coastlines and mark dangerous shoals. These towers became symbols of safety and resilience, often manned by dedicated keepers who maintained the lights and fog signals. As maritime technology advanced, however, the need for human operation began to decline.
